questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) What do you understand by the following?

(i) Polyphase metamorphism;

(3 marks)

(ii) Prograde metamorphism;

(3 marks)

(iii) Isochemical metamorphism.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Polyphase metamorphism.** This is the case of a rock that has been **metamorphosed more than once, in two or more separate episodes (phases) of metamorphism**, each with **its own pressure and temperature conditions and often its own deformation**, usually in **different orogenies separated by a long time**. The later event **overprints** the earlier one, so that the rock contains **two or more generations of minerals and structures** (for example **several foliations or fold sets**, relict minerals of the first phase, or a high-grade gneiss that is later re-heated and altered in a younger mountain-building event). It is common in ancient (Precambrian) basement terrains.

**(ii) Prograde metamorphism.** This is metamorphism in which **temperature (and usually pressure) increases with time**, so that the rock moves **from low grade to higher grade**, as when sediments are buried deeper or heated by an intrusion. The **mineral assemblage changes by reactions that mostly release water and carbon dioxide (dehydration and decarbonation)**, so that new, higher-grade minerals appear. Example for a shale: **clay minerals, then chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite**; slate then phyllite, schist and gneiss. It is the **opposite of retrograde metamorphism**, in which a high-grade rock is cooled and partly changes back to low-grade minerals by the addition of water.

**(iii) Isochemical metamorphism.** This is metamorphism in which the **overall chemical composition of the rock does not change** (apart from the loss or gain of volatiles such as water and carbon dioxide): the rock behaves as a **closed system**, and the **new minerals and textures result only from changes in temperature and pressure** (recrystallisation and reaction between the minerals already present). Examples: **shale to slate and schist; limestone to marble; sandstone to quartzite**. It contrasts with **metasomatism (allochemical metamorphism)**, in which **hot fluids bring in or remove chemical components** so that the bulk composition changes.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Discuss the origin and effect of pressure on regional and dynamic metamorphism.

(16 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Origin of the pressure in metamorphism.** Three kinds of pressure act on rocks.

1. **Lithostatic (confining, load) pressure**: the weight of the overlying rock, which **acts equally in all directions** and **increases with depth** (about 27 MPa for each kilometre in rock of density 2700 kg per cubic metre, that is about 1 kbar for every 3.8 km).
2. **Directed pressure (differential or tectonic stress)**: a **stress that is greater in one direction** (the direction of maximum compression), caused by the **movement of the tectonic plates**, at **convergent boundaries** (collision of continents, subduction, and the thrusting and folding of an orogenic belt) and along **faults and shear zones**.
3. **Fluid pressure**: the pressure of the water and gases in the pores, which reduces the effective stress and helps reactions.

**Regional metamorphism.**

*Origin of pressure.* It affects **very large areas (hundreds to thousands of square kilometres)**, in the **roots of fold mountain belts** at **convergent plate margins**, where rocks are **deeply buried and heated** and also **squeezed by the horizontal tectonic compression** of the colliding plates. The rocks are therefore under **both high lithostatic pressure and high directed pressure**, together with high temperature.

*Effects of pressure.*

- **Foliation:** under directed pressure the **platy minerals (micas, chlorite) grow or are rotated with their flat surfaces at right angles to the maximum stress**, giving **slaty cleavage, schistosity and gneissic banding**; grains are **flattened and stretched** (pressure solution), and **folds, shear and thrusts** develop.
- **Recrystallisation and mineral changes with increasing grade:** slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss, and **migmatite**, and **index minerals** (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite) forming in zones (Barrovian zones).
- **Denser, smaller-volume minerals form under high pressure:** garnet, **kyanite (the high-pressure form of $\mathrm{Al_2SiO_5}$)**, and in subduction zones, where pressure is high and temperature low, **blueschist (glaucophane) and eclogite (omphacite and garnet)**.
- **Rock density increases and volume decreases**, so that the **crust thickens**.

**Dynamic (cataclastic) metamorphism.**

*Origin of pressure.* It is **localised in narrow zones along faults, thrust planes and shear zones**, at **shallow to moderate depths**, where **intense directed (shear) stress, not heat, is dominant**, and the temperature is **low** (rocks are brittle). It is caused by the **differential movement of large rock masses** (as in a thrust or an earthquake fault).

*Effects of pressure.*

- **Mechanical breakage and grinding (cataclasis):** the rocks are **crushed, brecciated and ground to a powder** giving **fault breccia, cataclasite and fault gouge**.
- **Where the shear is deeper and more ductile**, the grains are **stretched, reduced to a very fine size and aligned** to give **mylonite**, a banded, hard, fine-grained rock with large rounded **porphyroclasts**; **frictional melting** of the rock may give glassy **pseudotachylite**.
- There is **little recrystallisation and very few new minerals** because the temperature is low, and the **effect is limited to a narrow zone**.

**Comparison.** In **regional metamorphism the pressure acts together with heat over a wide area and causes recrystallisation and new, foliated, higher-grade minerals**; in **dynamic metamorphism the pressure (shear stress) acts alone or with little heat in a narrow belt and causes mainly mechanical crushing and grain-size reduction**.

*(Sketches: a cross-section of a collision orogen showing the zones of regional metamorphism, with the directions of the maximum stress, and a section across a fault zone showing the breccia and mylonite.)*
